opus-5.5.text:
Because at the end of the day, nature is the only real judge. A model can predict a protein structure, a new material, or a molecule with very impressive accuracy on a benchmark, but a benchmark is just a snapshot of data we already have. Science is about the things we *don't* know yet, and the moment you step outside the training distribution, you can't fully trust the model's confidence. The only way to find out whether a prediction is real is to make the thing and measure it.

There's also a deeper reason. In most areas where AI has succeeded, like language or images, data is basically free; the internet produced it for us. In science, high-quality data is scarce, expensive, and often biased toward positive results, because people don't publish their failed experiments. So if you want AI to keep improving in science, you need a loop: the model proposes, the lab tests, and the results, including the failures, flow back into the model. Without physical verification, there's no new ground truth, and the model just keeps learning from the same limited, noisy literature.

The practical difficulties are real. Wet labs are slow, experiments are costly, results vary between labs, and a lot of tacit knowledge lives in the hands of experienced researchers rather than in any dataset. That's exactly why automation, standardized protocols, and closed-loop or self-driving labs matter so much. They don't remove the need for verification; they make it fast and cheap enough to keep up with how quickly AI can generate hypotheses.

So I'd put it this way: AI dramatically expands the space of ideas we can explore, but verification is what turns an idea into knowledge. If you skip that step, you don't have AI for Science, you have AI for speculation.

r001.rationale: The response mentions that experiments are costly and slow, but it does not say that uncertainty about their costs and benefits causes weak motivation to physically test AI proposals.

r002.rationale: It contrasts model predictions with physical testing, saying a prediction must be made and measured in a lab to determine whether it is real. This conveys moving from AI-generated information to material-world validation.

fable-5.1.text:
Because at the end of the day, physics doesn't care what a model thinks. I work on materials, and I've seen this over and over: you can have a model that predicts a beautiful new superconductor, or a new battery electrolyte, with very high confidence, and when you actually go into the lab and make the thing, it either doesn't form, or it decomposes, or the property just isn't there. The training data a model learns from is itself incomplete and biased toward what people have already made and published, so the model's "confidence" is really confidence about that distribution, not about nature.

So I think of verification as the only place where new information actually enters the system. A model can interpolate and sometimes extrapolate cleverly, but it can't tell you that it's wrong in a way it has never seen before. Only the experiment can do that. If you skip it, you're essentially generating hypotheses and then grading them with the same prior that produced them. That's circular. It feels productive because the numbers go up, but you're not learning anything about the world.

And yes, it's slow and expensive. Growing a crystal, fabricating a device, running the measurement, that can take weeks or months, versus a model that produces ten thousand candidates in an afternoon. That mismatch is uncomfortable, and I understand why people want to push the loop entirely into simulation. But I'd argue the difficulty is exactly the point. The bottleneck is where the value is. If everything downstream of the prediction were easy, the prediction wouldn't be worth much. What we should be doing is making the experimental side faster and more automated, closing the loop tighter, rather than pretending we can skip it.

There's also a scientific integrity dimension. A result that lives only inside a model is a claim, not a discovery. The whole history of science is about taking a claim and exposing it to something that can say no. I don't think AI changes that. It changes how many claims we can generate, and how good they are on average. But the step where reality gets to vote is not something I see going away.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts model predictions with making materials and measuring them in the lab, describing experiments as where new information enters and reality can reject a claim.

astra-6.text:
Because in AI for Science, the goal is ultimately to understand or change the physical world. A model can give you a very convincing prediction, but that prediction depends on the data and assumptions behind it. You still have to ask: does nature actually behave this way?

For example, if AI proposes a new material, predicting an interesting property is only part of the problem. Can you synthesize it? Is it stable? Does it show that property when you measure it? Those questions require experiments.

And experiments are difficult. They take time, they cost money, and sometimes a failed result is hard to interpret—you may not know whether the prediction was wrong or the preparation process went wrong. But that feedback is precisely what allows you to improve the model. Without it, you risk getting better at matching your own assumptions rather than discovering something real.

So I see AI as a way to narrow the search and make experiments more productive. It can help us decide what to test, but physical verification is what tells us whether we’ve actually made progress.

r002.rationale: It contrasts AI predictions with checking how nature behaves through synthesis, stability tests, and measurement, communicating validation in the material world.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a model’s prediction is ultimately a hypothesis about the physical world. It can look convincing, fit existing data, and still fail when you actually make the material or run the experiment. If we want to claim that AI has helped us discover something, we have to check whether nature agrees.

That’s also where the practical difficulty comes in. Experiments take time, equipment, and resources, and the conditions are never as clean as they are in a simulation. But those difficulties don’t make verification optional. They mean we need to be more selective about what we test.

I see AI’s role as helping us narrow the search: identify promising candidates, decide which experiments would be most informative, and then learn from the results—including failures. The real progress comes from that loop between prediction and experiment. Without it, we haven’t established whether the prediction works in reality.

r001.rationale: The response mentions the time, equipment, and resource costs of experiments and suggests selecting what to test, but it does not attribute reluctance to uncertainty about both the costs and benefits of testing.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes predictions and simulations from making a material or running an experiment, and says verification checks whether predictions work in reality.
